payload.name: Expand stress-reliever queries with calming activity vocabulary
payload.description: When a question asks what someone does to relieve stress or what their stress relievers are, also search for calming/peaceful activity memories before answering.
content: When a question asks what a person's stress relievers are or what they do to relieve stress, do not search only the literal phrase 'stress reliever' or 'stress'. Run additional searches using calming and outcome vocabulary: 'relax', 'relaxing', 'calm', 'calming', 'finds peace', 'peaceful', 'de-stress', 'unwind', 'helps <person> relax'.

Also search preference and event memories for hobbies and nature/view activities (e.g., sunsets, scenic places, landscapes), because calming activities are often stored without the word 'stress'. If the retrieved evidence does not include any memory that explicitly describes a relaxing or calming activity, issue a varied supplementary search before answering.

candidates.solves: Questions about a person's stress relievers are often answered by memories phrased as 'relaxing', 'finds peace', or 'calming activity', which a literal 'stress reliever' search misses. This skill generalizes that mechanism by requiring calming-synonym expansion and supplementary retrieval of hobby and nature/view activities before answering. It applies to any future access query asking what relieves stress or calms a person, not to identifying sources of stress.

payload.name: Search teaching and sharing memories broadly
payload.description: When a question asks what skills, abilities, or knowledge a person helped others learn, taught, or shared, search beyond literal 'helped learn' phrasing and across domains before answering.
content: If the question asks which skills a person helped others learn, taught, or shared, run searches using both explicit teaching/helping terms (taught, helped learn, trained, coached) and sharing/enthusiasm terms (shared, introduced, passionate about, showed others), because memories often record 'sharing a passion' rather than 'teaching a skill'.
Include profile and preference memories in these searches, not only event memories; a person's interest or hobby memory may record that they share it with others.

Before answering an enumeration question, check whether retrieved evidence is concentrated in one domain; if so, run additional searches for the person's other hobbies, interests, and activities so the answer does not miss skills from other domains.

candidates.solves: The Access Agent answered an enumeration question about skills a person helped others learn using only explicit event memories, missing a profile memory where the person 'shared a passion' for another skill. The reusable mechanism is lexical mismatch between literal teach/help wording and memory phrasing, plus premature stopping after finding hits in one domain. Future questions asking what someone taught, helped others learn, or shared with others should trigger broader teaching/sharing vocabulary and cross-domain searches before answering.

payload.name: Concrete-synonym expansion for abstract action/space queries
payload.description: When a question describes a physical action or space with abstract/evaluative wording (e.g., 'fun indoor area', 'nice setup') and the first retrieval misses relevant memories, use concrete functional synonyms and re-search before concluding no information.
content: If a question describes a physical action or space using abstract, colloquial, or evaluative terms (e.g., 'fun indoor area', 'safe spot', 'nice setup'), do not stop after searching only those literal terms; run additional searches using concrete functional vocabulary a stored memory would likely contain (e.g., 'set up', 'space', 'bed', 'toys', 'supplies', 'indoor') combined with the person/entity and any known objects.

When the initial retrieval returns only superficially related memories and none explicitly describes the target action/space, issue at least one more search with different concrete synonyms or structured predicates before answering 'no information'.
If a retrieved memory describes the same concrete setup/activity with different wording, treat it as candidate evidence and use its temporal field to answer 'when' questions.

candidates.solves: When a question describes an action or physical space using abstract, evaluative, or colloquial wording (e.g., 'fun indoor area') while the stored memory uses concrete functional terms (e.g., 'setting up a safe space with bed and toys'), the agent retrieves only superficially related memories and wrongly answers 'no information'. The reusable rule is to expand abstract action/space queries with concrete functional synonyms and to re-search before concluding absence of evidence, applying to any retrieval where the target is a physical arrangement or activity described with paraphrased language.

payload.name: Per-person retrieval for multi-subject questions
payload.description: When a question asks about the views, feelings, or experiences of multiple named people on a shared topic, and initial retrieval covers only some of them, run per-person searches before answering.
content: If a question asks why or how multiple named people relate to a common topic, treat an initial search as insufficient when it returns memories about only a subset of those people.

Run at least one additional hybrid or keyword search for each named person combined with the common topic and relevant predicate terms (e.g., '<person> <predicate> <topic>'), because relevant memories may be buried in enrichment records whose primary object is unrelated.

Before answering, verify that the retrieved evidence addresses every person named in the question; if any person still lacks evidence after expanded searches, state that explicitly instead of generalizing from other people's memories.

candidates.solves: Questions asking why multiple named people share a view or experience often retrieve evidence for only a subset, leading to premature answers from partial evidence. In the diagnosed case, a relevant memory existed for the omitted person but was buried in an enrichment record with a different primary object, so a single query did not surface it. The rule to run per-person searches and verify coverage transfers to any multi-subject question about admiration, preferences, opinions, or shared events.

payload.name: Broaden retrieval for shared-activity questions
payload.description: When a question asks what two people do together, do not restrict the search to queries containing both names and the word 'together'; also search each person's individual activities because joint activities are often stored under one participant.
content: If a question asks what two people do together (e.g., 'What do X and Y do together?'), do not rely only on a query that includes both names and 'together'; that over-constrains retrieval and misses memories stored under one person.

Run additional searches using each person's name alone with generic activity terms (e.g., '[X] activities', '[Y] hobbies'), and include memory kinds event, preference, and profile so individual activity memories can surface.

Before answering 'no information available', inspect whether any retrieved memory about one person's activities could describe an activity shared with the other person, and if needed retry with broader terms or higher top_k.

candidates.solves: The retrieval failed because the query was built entirely around both participant names plus 'together', so memories stored under only one participant's activities were not retrieved. This over-constraining pattern recurs whenever a question asks what two people do together, but the memory records the activity for one person. The rule applies to future shared-activity or joint-hobby questions: supplement pair-specific wording with per-person activity searches and generic activity terms before concluding the information is absent.

payload.name: Per-person searches for multi-person activity questions
payload.description: When a question asks what ways, methods, or items multiple people use for an activity, run a separate search for each named person before answering.
content: When a question asks for the ways, methods, or items two or more people use for an activity (e.g., enhance, improve, enjoy their practice), do not rely only on a single joint query with all names. Run at least one hybrid search per person, combining that person's name with the activity and preference-oriented terms such as 'prefers', 'uses', 'likes', 'enjoys', 'enhances'.

Include 'preference' and 'event' memory kinds in these per-person searches, since relevant details are often stored as individual preferences or purchase/use events that do not mention the other person.

Before answering, verify that each named person has at least one retrieved memory about the activity and its enhancement; if not, issue an additional targeted search for that person before finalizing the answer.

candidates.solves: Joint multi-person queries about an activity can miss person-specific preference and event memories, causing answers to omit one person's methods. This rule applies when a question asks for the ways, methods, or items multiple people use for a shared activity: run a separate search for each person to surface evidence stored individually. It does not apply to single-person activity questions or to recommendation-from-one-person questions.

payload.name: SearchOwnedItemAttributeSynonyms
payload.description: When a question asks for a specific attribute (e.g., breed, make, model) of a person's pets or possessions, and the first search returns only ownership or activity memories, run additional synonym-value searches and inspect profile memories before answering.
content: When a question asks for a specific attribute of a person's pets or possessions (e.g., breeds, makes, models, colors) and the first hybrid search returns only generic ownership, care, or activity memories, treat the evidence as insufficient instead of answering from those memories.

Run at least one additional search using synonym or value terms for the queried attribute even if they do not appear in the question (e.g., for breeds: 'mix', 'mongrel', 'purebred', common breed names; for vehicles: 'make', 'model', 'year', brand names).

Inspect the subject's profile memories and their versions for explicit attribute statements, and answer only when a memory directly states the attribute values; do not infer names or breeds from non-specific ownership memories.

candidates.solves: Literal retrieval missed a profile memory where the requested attribute is stored as value wording (e.g., 'Lab mix' rather than 'breeds'), causing a premature answer from a generic ownership memory. The reusable rule is to run synonym/value searches for the queried attribute of owned entities and inspect profile memories before answering. It applies to future questions asking for specific attributes (breed, make, model, color) of a person's pets or possessions.

payload.name: Expand collection enumeration searches
payload.description: Use when a question asks what items a person collects or gathers; expand search vocabulary beyond 'collect' and enumerate all named collectible items from preference and event memories.
content: If a question asks what items a person collects or gathers, do not query only with 'collect(s)'. Also run supplementary searches using '<person> collection', '<person> hobbies', '<person> interests', '<person> likes', '<person> enjoys', and '<person> favorite'.

If a retrieved memory mentions a specific collectible category (e.g., jerseys, DVDs, shoes, memorabilia) or a related hobby/media interest, search for that item term with the person's name before finalizing.

Before answering, enumerate all distinct named collectible items from preference and event memories, and if the retrieved set seems incomplete (e.g., only one item for a plural 'items' question), run at least one additional vocabulary-expanded search.

candidates.solves: A verb-only 'collect' search missed equally valid 'collection', 'enjoys', or hobby/media phrasings, yielding an incomplete item list. The mechanism is a lexical gap: enumeration questions need vocabulary-expanded, exhaustive preference-memory searching. Applies to any future question asking what items a person collects/gathers; not to count questions or single-item factoids.

payload.name: Complete shared-category item lists after partial hits
payload.description: Use when a question asks for all named items in a category shared by two entities and the first search returns some but not necessarily all such items.
content: When answering a question that asks for a complete list of named items shared by two entities, treat the first retrieval's named items as a partial set, not a complete answer.

Before answering, run additional searches combining each entity with category activity verbs (plays, recommends, enjoys, bought) and with each already-found item name to surface differently phrased memories.
Inspect preference, hobby, recommendation, and event memories in addition to direct co-activity memories, and stop only when additional varied searches yield no new named items.

candidates.solves: A broad hybrid search returned a partial list of shared items and the agent answered immediately, missing a differently phrased memory that named an additional item. The mechanism is treating an initial partial item list as exhaustive for category-intersection questions. A rule to continue with per-entity activity-term and per-item searches until no new instances appear applies to any future 'which X do they share/play/watch/read together' query.

payload.name: Family-member expansion for who-in-family questions
payload.description: When a question asks who in a person's family experienced a condition or event, run supplementary searches for each family role combined with the condition before answering.
content: When a question asks who in a person's family has or experienced a condition/event (e.g., injured, sick, plays a sport), do not conclude from the named person's own memories alone.

First retrieve relationship memories to identify known family roles (son, partner, parents, etc.), then run additional searches combining each role with the condition/event terms (e.g., '<person> son <condition>').
If a family role has no matching memory after these searches, then it is safe to answer from the retrieved evidence; otherwise keep searching.

candidates.solves: A diagnosis of a family-level question (e.g., who was injured) showed that the agent retrieved only the named person's injury and missed a family member's injury stored in a separate memory. The rule to expand queries across family roles generalizes to any question asking who among a person's relatives has a condition, activity, or attribute, because such memories are often filed per individual rather than under the family unit.

payload.name: CompleteItemEnumerationWithVariedSearches
payload.description: When a question asks what books, movies, shows, or other items a person has read/watched/consumed, run multiple varied searches and inspect additional memories before answering, even if the first search returned some named items.
content: When a question asks for a list of items a person has read, watched, liked, or consumed (books, movies, series, foods, etc.), do not treat a single search that returns some named items as complete.

Before answering, run at least one additional hybrid or keyword search combining the subject's name with alternative activity terms and related subtypes (e.g., 'finished', 'enjoyed', 'mentioned', 'recommended', 'series', 'non-fiction', 'reads') to retrieve memories that name items without using the exact category noun.
Inspect both event and preference memories from these additional searches, and only produce the final list after no further varied search surfaces additional named items.

candidates.solves: For enumeration questions about a person's read/watched/consumed items, a single literal search is insufficient even if it returns some named items, because relevant memories may phrase items as 'finished a fantasy series' or 'enjoys non-fiction books'. The rule requires additional varied searches before answering. It applies to any item-list question (books, movies, shows, foods); it does not apply to single-item, yes/no, or count-only questions.

payload.name: Explicit role evidence for joined team queries
payload.description: When a query asks for a person's position, role, or title on a team or organization they signed with, joined, or were hired into, search signing/joining memories and require explicit role evidence before answering.
content: If a question asks for a person's position/role/title on a team or organization they signed with, joined, or were hired into, run searches combining the person's name with role terms ('position', 'role', 'title') and joining terms ('signed with', 'joined', 'hired as', 'drafted by'); do not restrict memory_kinds, and include plan and event memories since such facts are often stored there.

Before answering a role/position question, require evidence that explicitly names the role (e.g., 'as a [role]', 'hired as [role]'); do not infer a formal position from related activities such as mentoring, playing, or volunteering, and do not stop at the first semantically related memory.

If the first search returns no memory that explicitly assigns a role, retry with alternate role and joining phrasings, including the specific team/organization name from the question, before finalizing an answer.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for a person's formal position, role, or title on a team or organization they signed with or joined, the supporting fact is often stored in a signing/joining plan or event memory, not in activity or preference memories. The diagnosed failure was answering from a related activity memory because the explicit role memory was not retrieved. This rule transfers to any similar role/position query by requiring targeted searches for joining terminology and explicit role evidence before answering.

payload.name: Search recipe and meal terms for cooked-dish enumerations
payload.description: When a question asks what a person has cooked, made, or prepared, run searches for recipe-sharing and habitual-cooking event memories using terms like recipe, dish, meal, and often makes.
content: If the question asks for a list of dishes a person has cooked/made/prepared, include at least one query expansion with 'recipe', 'dish', 'meal', or 'often makes' in addition to 'cooked'/'made'.

Do not stop after a search that returns only generic cooking activity or a single direct dish; continue with recipe-oriented terms and inspect event memories where the person shares a recipe or is described as frequently making a dish.
When enumerating, include concrete dishes from recipe-sharing and habitual-cooking event memories as evidence, and answer only from retrieved memory content.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for an enumeration of dishes a person has cooked, made, or prepared, direct searches for 'cooked' or 'made' can miss memories where the person shares a recipe or is described as often making a specific dish. This rule adds recipe/meal-oriented searches and includes those event memories before answering. It applies to future cook/make/prepare enumeration questions, not to ownership counts or preference-only lists.

payload.name: Saturate-search-before-answering-ownership-counts
payload.description: Use when a question asks how many items a person owns/has and the first search returns some named item instances; do not stop before all distinct instances are found.
content: When counting items a person owns/has, treat any single retrieval as partial evidence: it often names only some of the person's items while other acquisition/ownership memories exist separately.

Before answering, issue follow-up searches with acquisition/ownership verbs (adopted, bought, received, got, owns) and the names of items already found, plus singular/plural object forms, until consecutive searches surface no new distinct item instance.
Pool evidence across all retrieved memories before finalizing: enumerate every distinct named item attributed to the person, and only sum them after search saturation confirms the set is complete.

candidates.solves: When counting items a person owns/has, a single retrieval often returns only a subset of the owned instances; separate acquisition memories for other items exist but are missed because the agent stops after the first partial count. This rule forces iterative, saturation-based searching using acquisition verbs and the names of already-found items before summing, and applies to any future 'how many X does Y own/have' question.

payload.name: Include profile memories for favorite-category questions
payload.description: When a question asks for a person's favorite genre/category of movies, books, shows, or similar, include profile memories in retrieval; do not limit to event and preference memories.
content: If the question asks for a person's favorite genre, category, or general preference (movies, books, shows, foods, hobbies), run the initial search without a restrictive memory_kind filter, or explicitly include 'profile' alongside 'preference' and 'event'.

When the first search returns no explicit genre/category, repeat the search with query expansions using terms like 'enjoys', 'likes', 'interest', and 'favorite genre', and inspect profile memories because they often combine multiple stated preferences.
Before answering 'No information available', verify that profile memories containing the subject's stated likes or enjoyments were retrieved and inspected.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for a person's favorite genre or category (movies, books, shows, foods, hobbies), restricting retrieval to event and preference memory kinds can miss profile memories that explicitly state the preference. The diagnosed failure occurred because the agent searched only preference/event kinds and therefore missed a profile memory stating the person enjoys fantasy and sci-fi movies. This rule applies to any future favorite-category question where preference evidence may be stored in profile memories, so retrieval must not exclude that kind.

payload.name: SearchGroupEventMemoriesForOtherFriends
payload.description: When a question asks whether a person has friends, teammates, or social connections besides/apart from a named person, include event and group-participation memories; do not restrict to relationship memories or the word 'friend'.
content: When a question asks whether someone has friends or social connections besides, apart from, or other than a named person, do not restrict retrieval to memory_kind 'relationship' or to queries containing only 'friend'.

Run at least one search over event (and optionally profile/relationship) memories using group-participation terms (team, teammate, club, tournament, group, class, colleague, coworker) with the subject's name, and omit the named excluded person from the query and keywords.

If initial results only describe the named relationship, broaden memory_kinds and re-query with additional group/activity expansions before concluding the person has no other friends; event memories of team or group participation can imply other social connections.

candidates.solves: The Access Agent answered 'no friends besides X' after restricting searches to relationship memories and the word 'friend', missing an event memory implying teammates. Abstractly, questions about a person's social circle beyond a named person require event/group-participation evidence, not just relationship memories. Future 'besides/apart from' friendship questions should trigger broader memory-kind searches; activity-enumeration questions are outside this skill.

payload.name: Include profile memories for joined classes and groups
payload.description: When asking what classes, courses, workshops, or groups a person has joined, enrolled in, or participates in, use profile memory kind alongside event/plan and count sign-ups as joined.
content: When the question asks about classes, courses, workshops, or groups a person joined, enrolled in, or participates in, do not restrict memory_kinds to event/plan; include profile memories too, since memberships and group participation are often stored as profile enrichments.
Treat 'signed up for', 'enrolled in', 'joined', or 'registered for' an activity as evidence of joining, even when it is scheduled to start in the future.
After retrieval, enumerate every distinct class/course/workshop/group named in any retrieved memory; do not omit a concrete one that appeared in results.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what classes, courses, workshops, or groups a person joined or participates in, agents often restrict searches to event/plan memories and miss profile-stored memberships, and may ignore a retrieved sign-up because it starts in the future. This rule generalizes to any membership/enrollment question: include profile memories and treat enrollments/sign-ups as joined, then enumerate every named class/group found.

payload.name: Retrieve plan memories for creative work inspiration
payload.description: When a question asks what inspired or motivated a person's creative work or ongoing project, include plan memories in searches and do not restrict to event memories alone.
content: When a question asks what inspired, motivated, or caused a person's creative work or ongoing project (screenplay, book, film, or similar), do not restrict retrieval to 'event' memory kind; include 'plan' memories, since in-progress works and their stated reasons are often stored as plans.

Run additional searches pairing the work's terms with inspiration/motivation phrasing and generic descriptors ('creative project', 'new work', 'recent project') across all memory kinds, and use keyword or date-filtered queries when a specific date is given.

Before answering, require a retrieved memory that directly states the inspiration; if only circumstantial evidence (e.g., media the person consumed) is found, keep searching with broader memory kinds instead of inferring the inspiration.

candidates.solves: The agent restricted searches to event memories and missed the plan memory directly stating what inspired the screenplay, inferring instead from a circumstantial favorite film. The reusable mechanism is over-restricting memory kinds on motivation questions; apply whenever a question asks for the inspiration or reason behind a creative work or ongoing project, not to factual event or completed-work-subject questions.

payload.name: Include preference memories for recently-finished-activity queries
payload.description: When a question asks what someone just finished reading, watching, playing, or otherwise recently completed, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'event'; include 'preference' and 'state' because completed favorites are often stored as preference memories.
content: If a user asks what a person recently finished or just completed (e.g., a book, show, game, project), set memory_kinds to include both 'event' and 'preference' (or omit the filter), because such completed items are often stored as preference memories rather than event memories.

When the question combines a completion verb ('finished', 'just read', 'completed') with a concrete date, do not limit retrieval only to event memories on that date; run an additional search without a memory_kinds restriction or with 'preference' included so that preference memories with a matching world_start can surface.

Before answering 'no information available' for a completed-activity question, check whether any retrieved preference or state memory explicitly states the completed item, even if no event memory matches.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed failure: an agent asked what book a person just finished reading on a specific date, restricted memory_kinds to 'event', and missed the preference memory that contained the completed book. The abstract mechanism is over-restricting memory_kinds to event for completion queries, even though recently completed activities and items are often stored as preference memories. This rule applies to any future question about a recently finished or completed activity/artifact and prevents premature 'no information' answers.

payload.name: Retrieve favorite items via shared-activity and preference memories
payload.description: When a question asks for a person's favorite item with a specific attribute, and a direct search using the attribute and 'favorite' misses the memory, search the person's item-sharing and preference memories before concluding no information.
content: When a question asks for a person's favorite item with a specific attribute (e.g., a dish including garlic), do not require the attribute word or 'favorite' to appear verbatim in a memory. Run an additional hybrid search pairing the person with the item's activity/category terms (recipes, cooking, sharing meals) and inspect current versions of top results.

If a retrieved event describes the item with other descriptors and a separate memory records the person's preference for the queried attribute, use the combination as evidence instead of answering 'No information available' simply because no single memory contains all query terms.

Match the queried date against memories' structured world_start/world_end, not against the date phrase in the text; a memory whose world_start equals the queried date can be the sharing/offering event.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for a person's favorite item with an attribute, direct searches requiring the attribute word or 'favorite' can miss memories describing the item differently. The agent then answers 'No information available' despite separate evidence: an event of sharing/offering the item and a preference memory for the attribute. The rule: combine distributed event and preference evidence before concluding absence. Applies to favorite-item-with-attribute questions; not for questions without a specific attribute or direct evidence.
